meta.title: Vehicle on a Banked Road: Smooth & Rough Banking Dynamics

seo.title: Vehicle on a Banked Road With and Without Friction JEE Main DPP-034 | SMA Physics
seo.description: 20 High-yield JEE Main MCQ practice questions covering optimum design speed, friction-assisted upper and lower safe speed limits, normal force calculation, railway track elevation (superelevation), and infinite speed threshold condition.
seo.keywords: JEE Main Physics, Banked Road DPP, Banking with Friction, Optimum Speed Curve, Minimum Safe Speed Banked Road, Superelevation Railway, Syed Mazhar Ali, SMA Physics

conceptCapsule.title: Road Banking Mechanics, Friction Direction & Speed Boundaries
conceptCapsule.summary: 1. Ideal Design Speed (Frictionless Banking): On a track of radius $R$ banked at angle $	heta$, the horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripetal acceleration ($N\sin\theta = \frac{mv_0^2}{R}$ and $N\cos\theta = mg$), yielding $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$ with normal reaction $N = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$. 2. Rough Banked Road ($v > v_0$): When speed exceeds design speed, the car tends to skid uphill, so static friction $f_s$ acts downhill along the slope. The upper safe speed limit is $v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}\right]}$. If $\mu_s\tan\theta \ge 1$, $v_{\text{max}} \to \infty$. 3. Rough Banked Road ($v < v_0$): When speed is below design speed, the car tends to slide down the bank, so static friction acts uphill along the slope. The lower safe speed limit is $v_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{\tan\theta - \mu_s}{1 + \mu_s\tan\theta}\right]}$. If $\mu_s \ge \tan\theta$, $v_{\text{min}} = 0$. 4. Superelevation of Railway Tracks: Outer rail elevation is given by $h \approx d\tan\theta = \frac{v^2 d}{Rg}$, where $d$ is gauge distance.
conceptCapsule.examTrap: Remember that on a banked road, the direction of static friction depends strictly on whether the actual speed $v$ is greater or less than the ideal design speed $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$. If $v = v_0$, friction is zero. If $v > v_0$, friction points DOWN the incline. If $v < v_0$, friction points UP the incline.

questions.statement: A circular highway curve of radius $R = 200\text{ m}$ is banked for a design speed of $v_0 = 72\text{ km/h}$. If the road is assumed to be completely smooth, the banking angle $\theta$ of the curve is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Speed in SI units: $v_0 = 72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 20\text{ m/s}$.
For smooth banking: $$\tan\theta = \frac{v_0^2}{Rg} = \frac{20^2}{200 \times 10} = \frac{400}{2000} = 0.2 \implies \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.2)$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: On a frictionless banked circular track of radius $R$ and inclination $\theta$, the normal reaction force exerted by the road on a car of mass $m$ travelling at the design speed $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$ is:
questions.solution:
Vertical equilibrium gives $N\cos\theta = mg \implies N = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A circular road of radius $R = 40\text{ m}$ is banked at an angle $\theta = 45^\circ$. If the coefficient of static friction between tyres and the road is $\mu_s = 0.5$, the maximum speed $v_{\text{max}}$ with which a car can round the curve without skidding up the incline is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
$$v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{\tan 45^\circ + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan 45^\circ}\right]} = \sqrt{400\left[\frac{1 + 0.5}{1 - 0.5}\right]} = \sqrt{400 \times 3} = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.64\text{ m/s}$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: In Question 3, the minimum speed $v_{\text{min}}$ below which the car tends to slide down the banked incline is:
questions.solution:
$$v_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{\tan 45^\circ - \mu_s}{1 + \mu_s\tan 45^\circ}\right]} = \sqrt{400\left[\frac{1 - 0.5}{1 + 0.5}\right]} = \sqrt{\frac{400}{3}} \approx 11.55\text{ m/s}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: If the coefficient of static friction between the road and tyres is $\mu_s$, a parked car will remain safely at rest on a banked road without sliding down only if the banking angle $\theta$ satisfies:
questions.solution:
For a stationary vehicle ($v = 0$), static friction balances gravity along the slope if $mg\sin\theta \le \mu_s mg\cos\theta \implies \tan\theta \le \mu_s \implies \theta \le \tan^{-1}(\mu_s)$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A circular road track has a radius of curvature $R$ and is banked at an angle $\theta$. If the friction coefficient is $\mu_s$, the expression for the maximum permissible speed $v_{\text{max}}$ without upward slipping is:
questions.solution:
At maximum speed, friction acts down the slope: $N\sin\theta + f_s\cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{R}$ and $N\cos\theta - f_s\sin\theta = mg$. Solving with $f_s = \mu_s N$ gives $v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}\right]}$.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: From Question 6, if the banking angle $\theta$ and friction coefficient $\mu_s$ satisfy $\mu_s\tan\theta = 1$, the theoretical maximum safe speed $v_{\text{max}}$ before the car slips up the bank becomes:

options.text: Infinitely large (the vehicle never slips upwards)

questions.solution:
When $\mu_s\tan\theta = 1$, the denominator $(1 - \mu_s\tan\theta) = 0$, making $v_{\text{max}} \to \infty$. The normal force and friction increase proportionally with speed such that slipping up the bank never occurs at any speed.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A train rounds a horizontal circular curve of radius $R = 900\text{ m}$ at speed $v = 30\text{ m/s}$. The distance between the railway rails is $d = 1.5\text{ m}$. To prevent lateral thrust on the wheel flanges, the outer rail must be elevated above the inner rail by height $h$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
$$h \approx d\tan\theta = \frac{v^2 d}{Rg} = \frac{30^2 \times 1.5}{900 \times 10} = \frac{900 \times 1.5}{9000} = 0.15\text{ m}$$
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A car travels along a banked circular track at a speed $v$ that is strictly greater than the ideal design speed $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$. The direction of the frictional force exerted by the road on the tyres is:

options.text: Downwards along the inclined surface of the road
Upwards along the inclined surface of the road

questions.solution:
When $v > v_0$, the component of normal force $N\sin\theta$ alone cannot supply sufficient centripetal force. The vehicle tends to drift outwards and upwards, so static friction acts downwards along the inclined surface to assist centripetal acceleration.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A circular turn of radius $R = 50\text{ m}$ is banked at $\theta = 30^\circ$. A car of mass $m = 1000\text{ kg}$ is driven around the curve at the optimum speed ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). The magnitude of the normal force exerted on the car is:
questions.solution:
$$N = \frac{mg}{\cos 30^\circ} = \frac{1000 \times 10}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \frac{20000}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 11547\text{ N}$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A race car travels at $v = 50\text{ m/s}$ along a circular banked track of radius $R = 250\text{ m}$. If the banking angle is $\theta = 45^\circ$, the frictional force on the car of mass $m = 1200\text{ kg}$ is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Design speed for this banking: $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan 45^\circ} = \sqrt{250 \times 10 \times 1} = 50\text{ m/s}$. Since the car is travelling at exactly the design speed, no lateral slipping tendency exists, so the frictional force is zero.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A vehicle negotiates a banked curve of radius $R$ at speed $v < \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$ with $\mu_s > \tan\theta$. The magnitude of the static friction force developed is:
questions.solution:
For $v < v_0$, the car tends to slide down. Balancing forces along the incline: $mg\sin\theta - f = m\left(\frac{v^2}{R}\right)\cos\theta \implies f = m\left(g\sin\theta - \frac{v^2}{R}\cos\theta\right)$.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A road has a width $w = 10\text{ m}$ and a curve of radius $R = 50\text{ m}$. It is designed for safe travel at $v = 10\text{ m/s}$ without friction. The height by which the outer edge of the road must be raised is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
1. $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{Rg} = \frac{100}{500} = 0.2$.
2. $\sin\theta = \frac{0.2}{\sqrt{1 + 0.2^2}} = \frac{0.2}{\sqrt{1.04}} \approx 0.1961$.
3. Height $h = w\sin\theta = 10 \times 0.1961 \approx 1.96\text{ m}$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: For an unbanked flat road of radius $R$ ($\mu_s = 0.6$), the maximum safe speed is $v_1$. For a banked road of the same radius ($\theta = 37^\circ, \mu_s = 0.6$), the maximum safe speed is $v_2$. The ratio $v_2 / v_1$ is ($\sin 37^\circ = 0.6, \cos 37^\circ = 0.8$):
questions.solution:
1. $v_1 = \sqrt{\mu_s Rg} = \sqrt{0.6 Rg}$.
2. $\tan 37^\circ = 0.75 \implies v_2 = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{0.75 + 0.6}{1 - 0.75(0.6)}\right]} = \sqrt{Rg\left[\frac{1.35}{0.55}\right]} = \sqrt{2.4545 Rg}$.
3. Ratio: $\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\frac{2.4545}{0.6}} = \sqrt{4.09} \approx 2.0$.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: A bicyclist goes around a banked curve of radius $R = 20\text{ m}$ at speed $v = 10\text{ m/s}$. The road is banked at $\theta = 15^\circ$. To avoid side-thrust without friction, the angle $\alpha$ the cycle frame makes with the normal to the road surface is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Total angle required from vertical: $\tan\theta_{\text{total}} = \frac{v^2}{Rg} = \frac{100}{200} = 0.5 \implies \theta_{\text{total}} = 26.5^\circ$.
Lean angle relative to the road normal: $\alpha = 26.5^\circ - 15^\circ = 11.5^\circ$.
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: A curve of radius $R = 100\text{ m}$ is banked at angle $\theta = 30^\circ$. If the coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, the minimum speed $v_{\text{min}}$ to prevent the car from sliding down the incline is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Because $\mu_s = \tan 30^\circ$, we have $\mu_s = \tan\theta$. The numerator $(\tan\theta - \mu_s) = 0$, so $v_{\text{min}} = 0\text{ m/s}$. The vehicle will not slide down even if completely stopped.
Therefore, Option A is correct.

questions.statement: When a heavy truck and a lightweight sports car round the same smooth banked circular curve of radius $R$ and angle $	heta$ at the ideal design speed $v_0$:

options.text: The truck requires a higher speed because of its larger mass
Both vehicles negotiate the curve safely at the exact same speed $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$
The sports car requires a lower angle of banking
The truck experiences lower normal force

questions.solution:
The ideal design speed $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$ is completely independent of the mass of the vehicle.
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: A pendulum is suspended inside a car moving at ideal speed $v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}$ on a frictionless banked curve of inclination $	heta$. The angle made by the pendulum string with the normal to the banked road is:
questions.solution:
The effective gravity vector $\vec{g}_{\text{eff}} = \vec{g} - \vec{a}_c$ points at an angle $\tan\theta = a_c/g$ to the vertical, which is perpendicular to the banked road slope. Thus the pendulum string aligns along the normal ($0^\circ$).
Therefore, Option C is correct.

questions.statement: A car travels on a banked circular road of radius $R = 125\text{ m}$ and banking angle $	heta = 37^\circ$. If $\mu_s = 0.25$, the ratio of the maximum safe speed to the minimum safe speed $(v_{\text{max}} / v_{\text{min}})$ is ($\tan 37^\circ = 0.75$):
questions.solution:
$$\frac{v_{\text{max}}}{v_{\text{min}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\tan 37^\circ + \mu_s}{\tan 37^\circ - \mu_s} \cdot \frac{1 + \mu_s\tan 37^\circ}{1 - \mu_s\tan 37^\circ}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.75 + 0.25}{0.75 - 0.25} \cdot \frac{1 + 0.25(0.75)}{1 - 0.25(0.75)}} = \sqrt{2 \times \frac{1.1875}{0.8125}} \approx 1.71 \approx \sqrt{\frac{8}{3}}$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.statement: An aircraft is making a horizontal turn of radius $R = 2500\text{ m}$ at a constant speed of $v = 900\text{ km/h}$. The correct angle of banking $\theta$ of its wings to avoid lateral slipping is ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Speed in SI units: $v = 900 \times \frac{5}{18} = 250\text{ m/s}$.
$$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{Rg} = \frac{250^2}{2500 \times 10} = \frac{62500}{25000} = 2.5 \implies \theta = \tan^{-1}(2.5)$$
Therefore, Option B is correct.
